title: ADHD: assessment and practical support across daily life
intro: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, or ADHD, affects attention, impulse control and activity regulation. It begins in childhood, although some people are recognised only as adults. It is not established by being energetic, distracted during a stressful week or scoring highly on an internet checklist. Assessment considers persistent difficulties, development and their effects in different parts of life, alongside strengths and other possible explanations.

sections.heading: Describe patterns rather than blame behaviour
paragraphs: ADHD can involve losing track of tasks, forgetting belongings, difficulty waiting, interrupting or feeling restless. Some people mainly have attention difficulties without obvious hyperactivity. Notice when problems occur and how they affect learning, relationships, work and safety. Demanding settings can make difficulties more visible. Neither laziness nor poor parenting is an adequate explanation. At the same time, a particular behaviour alone cannot confirm ADHD; age, expectations and the environment matter.

sections.heading: Seek a comprehensive assessment
paragraphs: A clinician may gather developmental history and information from home, school or work, using questionnaires alongside interviews. There is no single blood test or scan that confirms ADHD. Sleep problems, anxiety, learning difficulties and other conditions can resemble or accompany it. Adults may benefit from old school reports or a relative's observations, if available, but should discuss missing records rather than assume assessment is impossible. Explain difficulties honestly, including coping strategies that hide the effort required.

sections.heading: Adapt tasks and surroundings while awaiting help
paragraphs: Support need not wait for a diagnostic label. Break a task into clear steps, reduce avoidable distractions and use visible reminders or a consistent place for essential items. Agree realistic routines with the person rather than imposing many changes at once. At school or work, discuss instructions in writing, planned breaks or a quieter setting. Review what actually helps; an adjustment that benefits one person may frustrate another. Recognise progress and avoid punishment for difficulties the person needs support to manage.

sections.heading: Compare support, skills approaches and medicines
paragraphs: The plan depends on age, impact, preferences and associated conditions. Parent support, behavioural approaches, education and psychological strategies can help with daily functioning. Medicines may also be appropriate after specialist assessment and discussion of benefits and harms. Before and during prescribing, the team reviews relevant physical and mental health, including heart history, sleep and appetite. Monitoring can include pulse, blood pressure and, in children, growth. Do not share medication, adjust doses alone or buy unverified products promising to cure ADHD.

sections.heading: Measure success by functioning and wellbeing
paragraphs: Agree specific goals, such as completing a morning routine with less conflict or managing deadlines more reliably. Review benefits, side effects and whether demands remain unrealistic. Tell the prescriber about significant mood changes, appetite or sleep problems; severe symptoms such as chest pain or fainting need urgent assessment. Difficulties can change with school transitions, employment or family responsibilities, so revisit support. ADHD may coexist with autism, depression or other conditions that deserve their own care rather than attributing every problem to ADHD.

examples.title: Hypothetical example: difficult mornings
examples.text: A child repeatedly misses steps when getting ready. The family and teacher help identify the pattern, and the family tries a short picture checklist with clothes prepared beforehand. They review whether this reduces stress while arranging assessment rather than labelling the child disobedient.

examples.title: Hypothetical example: adult difficulties
examples.text: An adult meets deadlines only by working late and feels exhausted. They describe both missed tasks and the hidden effort at assessment. Written priorities and scheduled check-ins at work are discussed alongside any treatment, instead of relying only on a questionnaire score.

questions: What supports the diagnosis, and what other explanations or coexisting conditions need assessment?
Which changes at home, school or work should we try and how will we judge their usefulness?
If medicine is considered, what benefits, side effects and monitoring should we expect?
